# Why Dharma belongs in the scholarly record

A name can be complete without carrying ​a single diacritic. **Dharma** is a canonical scholarly spelling, not a damaged form waiting for decoration. This post follows the evidence behind that spelling: the Devanagari record, the reconstructed sound, ‌the myths, the material culture, and the reasons this particular romanization became the public reference. The plain ASCII letters already contain the whole form. The scholarly work is to prove ‌their provenance, preserve their capitalization, and keep the name attached to its history.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Dharma
- **ASCII form:** dharma
- **Meaning:** "That which holds or sustains — ​law, duty, and righteousness; the moral and religious order that upholds the world (from √dhṛ, 'to hold, sustain')."
- **Domain of influence:** Law, Duty, Righteousness
- **Pantheon:** Sanskrit
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original ​script:** धर्म (Devanagari)

## Overview

**Dharma** (*dharma*) — That Which Holds, Law and Righteousness · That which holds or sustains — law, duty, and righteousness — belongs to the Sanskrit ​tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Law, Duty, Righteousness". The name means "That which holds or sustains — law, duty, and righteousness; the moral and religious order that ​upholds the world (from √dhṛ, 'to hold, sustain').".

**Dharma** is the load-bearing word of Indian civilization: the law that holds the cosmos, the duty that holds the person, the order ​that holds society. From √dhṛ, ‘to sustain’, it names everything that keeps the world from sliding into chaos — and in the epics it walks as a person: the ‌god of righteousness, father of Yudhiṣṭhira, who came down to test his own devotees.

PuniCodex records the canonical scholarly spelling **Dharma** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/dharma/). The displayed ​form is ASCII-equivalent — a description computed from the displayed form itself. The plain ASCII form *dharma* contains the same letters: no recovered diacritics or special encoding is claimed. ​The work here is consistent citation, capitalization, provenance, and cultural context.

## The Name

The name is attested in Devanagari as **धर्म**. Etymologically it means "That which holds or sustains — ‌law, duty, and righteousness; the moral and religious order that upholds the world (from √dhṛ, 'to hold, sustain').".

The canonical spelling **Dharma** matches the conventional scholarly romanization. The plain ASCII ​form *dharma* contains the same letters, so no lost diacritics or encoding transition is claimed. The editorial work is to fix one reviewed reference spelling, preserve capitalization and provenance, ‌and keep the original evidence visible. The displayed form is ASCII-equivalent — a description computed from the displayed form itself.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **d** → **D** — Same, capitalized

## The Original Script

The ‌name is preserved in Devanagari as **धर्म**.

The scholarly transliteration is *Dharma*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Sanskrit Dharma is written in Devanagari as धर्म
- IAST transliteration maps each ​Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
- Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of ​the name is **/ˈdɑːrmə/** — Sanskrit (IAST: Dharma).

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Dhar-** — The dh is a voiced aspirate — “d” with breath; the a is long “ah”.
- **-ma** ​— The word is the abstract noun from √dhṛ, “to hold, sustain” — that which holds the world up.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: “DAHR-muh”

Kindred and ​historical forms of the name:

- **Pāli** — Dhamma
- **Avestan** — daēnā (cognate family)

Not a god but a principle — personified as a god in the epics, whence this ​entry. In compounds the stem appears as dharma-; Middle Indic shortens it to dhamma-.

## Mythology

Dharma’s mythology is the epics’ moral machinery: the god of righteousness fathers the eldest Pāṇḍava, ‌tests his devotees in disguise, and — in the Nala story — teaches dice to a king as the instrument of ruin. He has no cult-image because he is what ​every cult-image stands for; yet the tradition gave him a family and a biography.

### The Father of Yudhiṣṭhira (Mahābhārata)

When Pāṇḍu was cursed to die on his wedding night, ‌his queens invoked the gods: Dharmarāja himself, the god of righteousness, fathered Yudhiṣṭhira on Kuntī. The eldest Pāṇḍava is thus dharma’s son — which is why the epic keeps asking ​whether righteousness itself can survive the dice-game and the war it forces.

### The Tests in Disguise (Dharma-Upākhyāna)

The epic’s forest-books stage Dharma’s examinations: as a stork demanding why Yudhiṣṭhira ‌would not abandon a fallen brother; as a Yakṣa whose riddles the king answers with the epic’s most quoted verses; as a dog who follows the Pāṇḍavas to heaven’s gate ​and is refused entry — until Yudhiṣṭhira refuses heaven without it. The dog was Dharma; the gate opens.

### The God Who Taught Dice (Nala Cycle)

In the Nala episode, Kali ‌— the demon of the Kali Yuga — begs Dharma for a means to enter the righteous king Nala; Dharma, inexplicably, teaches him dice. The story’s commentators wrestled for ​centuries with the god of righteousness arming the demon of strife: the standard resolution — even dharma’s permission is a test that righteousness must survive.

### The Son of Brahmā (Purāṇic ‌Personification)

The Purāṇas give Dharma genealogy: born of Brahmā’s breast as one of the mind-born sons, husband of Dhṛti and father of the personified virtues — Kāma (desire), Lobha ​(greed), Darpa (pride) and the rest. The abstraction’s family-tree is the Indian psyche’s map of its own forces.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Dharma concentrates in a small ​set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **The Load-Bearer** — The cosmos rests on dharma; the four feet of the bull of dharma mark the four ‌ages of time.
- **Duty by Caste and Stage** — Svadharma — one’s own duty by birth and life-stage: the Bhagavadgītā’s central teaching.
- **The Cosmic Ages** — The four yugas ‌are the four feet of the bull: four in the Kṛta age, one stumbling foot in ours.
- **The Tester of Men** — In the epics Dharma appears in disguise — ‌a beggar, a dog, a crane — to test righteousness where it counts.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The material record for Dharma survives in a small number of securely identified ​remains, catalogued below; the corpus is thin but unambiguous, and each site is tied to the name by ancient testimony.

Dharma’s monuments are juridical: the edict-pillars of Aśoka, whose dhamma ​inscriptions are the oldest deciphered moral legislation on earth. His wheel crowns the Indian flag; his bull — the dharmavṛṣabha — kneels on the seal of the Republic.

## Realm & ‌Domain

**Dharma** is the load-bearing word of Indian civilization: the law that holds the cosmos, the duty that holds the person, the order that holds society. From √dhṛ, ‘to ​sustain’, it names everything that keeps the world from sliding into chaos — and in the epics it walks as a person: the god of righteousness, father of Yudhiṣṭhira, who ​came down to test his own devotees.

The cosmos rests on dharma; the four feet of the bull of dharma mark the four ages of time.

## Across Cultures

Dharma and the Buddha’s Dhamma share a word and a mission: the Buddha claimed the title Dharmarāja, king of the law, and ‌made dharma’s wheel — the dharmacakra — his teaching’s emblem. The Zoroastrian daēnā and the Roman Fas are the comparison-points scholars cite; in India itself dharma absorbed every local law-code, ​from the Vedic ṛta to the medieval digests.

Within the Sanskrit tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[aditi|Aditi]], [[agni|Agni]], [[ambika|Ambikā]], [[amsa|Aṃśa]], [[arjuna|Arjuna]], and [[bhakti|Bhakti]].

## Cultural Legacy

The ‌word is untranslatable and indispensable — every rendering (‘law’, ‘duty’, ‘religion’, ‘righteousness’) is a fraction. The four feet of dharma’s bull are India’s theory of history; the Bhagavadgītā’s ‘better one’s ​own dharma, though defective’ is among the most quoted ethical sentences on earth. India’s modern name for itself, ‘Hindu Dharma’, keeps the word at the nation’s centre.

​The account of Dharma given in this edition rests on the witnesses and reference works listed below. Lexica and etymological dictionaries secure the form and meaning of the name; ​the literary and religious texts supply the narrative evidence.

## A Meditation

Dharma: the ​name of the thing that holds, restored in letters that hold nothing but carry everything. It needs no mark over its vowels — the word’s burden is its own ‌diacritic, the weight of the worlds it has held for four thousand years.

For **Dharma**, the chain begins with the attested form in Devanagari, continues through the standard scholarly ​romanizations, and ends with the canonical spelling used by this temple.
